Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
Wildlife Management Unit 354 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2019) 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 354 is a largely forested unit occurring within the dry mixedwood, central 
mixedwood and lower foothills subregions of west-central Alberta. In 1997 the unit was modified by splitting the 
larger former boundary of WMU 354 into smaller units, now identified as WMU 353 to the south and WMU 354 in 
the north. The modified area of WMU 354 is 2514 km 2, and the general boundary is delineated by the Forestry 
Trunk Road to the west, the Simonette River to the north and the Canfor 7000 Road to the south.  
The last survey for moose in WMU 354 was conducted in 2013 using distance sampling techniques. In 2013 the 
moose population was estimated to have 1618 individuals (90% CI 2204 - 3443), a density of 0.64 moose/km2, and 
a bull:cow:calf ratio of 23:100:28 (Table 1). Following this survey, the calf season, which was introduced in 1998, 
was removed. Antlered moose hunting is currently managed by special licence with a split season draw 
(September 24 to October 31; Novermber 1 to November 30), and an archery-only, non-draw licence season 
(August 25 to September 23). There is no antlerless moose season in this unit.  
The goal of the 2019 survey was to assess the status of moose since the last survey in 2013. Specific objectives 
were to determine a population estimate, population ratio for sex and age classes and a density estimate for 
moose in WMU 354. 
Survey Method 
An aerial survey for moose in WMU 354 was conducted from February 12 to 13, 2019. Distance sampling methods 
(Buckland et al., 2001) were used to determine moose population and density estimates. Distance sampling 
transects (n = 142), up to 10 kilometres in length and oriented north-south, were established throughout the unit 
with 1.8 kilometre spacing. A random sample of 47 transects was flown for a total survey effort of 423 kilometres. 
Moose were classified by age (adult or calf) and sex. Other wildlife observations were also recorded. 
 
Results 
One hundred and seventy-eight moose were observed in 121 independent groups. Of the 178 moose observed, 
170 individuals were successfully classified. Forty-eight (28%) were bulls, 96 (57%) were cows and 26 (15%) were 
calves. Of the bulls observed, 87% had already shed their antlers. Of the bulls still with antlers, two-thirds were 
small (small spike or forked antlers), and one-third were medium (small palmated antler ‘paddles’). No large bulls 
(large palmated antlers with minimum 3 points to the front with a spread more than half the body length) were 
observed. The bull:cow and calf:cow ratios were 0.50 and 0.27, respectively. The density estimate was 0.93 
moose/km2 with a coefficient of variation of 13%. The estimated moose population for WMU 354 is 2328 (90% CI 
1863 - 2909).  
We also observed 14 white-tailed deer (1 fawn and 13 unclassified), 9 elk (3 cows, 5 bulls and 1 calf) and 1 wolf, 
however these should not be considered minimum total counts as this survey method is unreliable for these 
species where the study area is in heavy forest cover or when populations are at low density.
